newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan 'triple bear' scenario said unlikely for now.
newsitem.headline: Japan 'triple bear' scenario said unlikely for now.

text.p: Japan's slumping stock market has renewed fears of a "triple bear" scenario in which Japan's currency, shares and bond prices all collapse at once.
But economists say that for now at least the feared market meltdown looks unlikely to materialise.

"You might get a total loss of confidence in which people sell every kind of Japanese asset, but that would require quite a dramatic worsening of sentiment," said Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Baring Securities in Tokyo.

Tokyo share prices have fallen relentlessly since late last year, in large part on the belief that the government was blithely implementing a fiscal belt-tightening policy that would halt Japan's economic recovery in its tracks.

The market's main barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, has slumped almost 14 percent since early December. The Nikkei closed down a steep 3.25 percent at 18,073.87 on Thursday, a drop of more than 600 points.

The yen also stumbled at the start of the year, briefly touching a nearly four-year low of 117 yen to the dollar on Monday, before Japanese officials jawboned it back up a bit with a spate of public comments earlier this week.

As it did late last year, the yen's decline sparked worries of a vicious cycle in which foreign investors would "sell Japan" by dumping stock and bond holdings rather than see the value of those assets decline further in their own currencies.
But economists said at the moment a currency-driven "triple bear" scenario looked unlikely.

"It's clearly a concern and the financial authorities are watching it. But the bond market isn't in a massive sell-off mode and they've sort of jawboned the currency market," said Ron Bevacqua, an economist at Merrill Lynch Japan. "As long as the yen depreciates slowly, I don't see a mad rush for the door in terms of foreign selling of Japanese bonds and equities."
Some stock market bears, however, worry that an unchecked share price decline could trigger a sell-off of bonds and the yen, a possibility economists said could not be ruled out.

"The more weakness there is in stocks, the greater the possibility that institutions would try to take profits in bonds to compensate for losses on stocks. The lower stocks go, the more people will consider that interest rates will stay low and take strength out of the currency as well," said Russell Jones, chief economist at Lehman Brothers in Tokyo.
"But we're some way away from this scenario at this stage," Jones added.

The gloomy outlook for Japan's economy, which is a big factor behind the share price slump, should in fact be a plus for bond prices, since it implies authorities will have to keep Japanese interest rates low, economists said.

"If the deterioration in the value of the currency and the fall in stocks is a reflection of the loss of confidence in the strength of the recovery, it should translate into better bond prices and lower yields," said Takashi Kiuchi, head of economic research at LTCB Research Institute.
Kiuchi said, however, that a "double bear" scenario of a weakening yen and falling share prices remained possible as long as market worries over Japan's economic outlook persisted.

Easing such worries would require Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) government to show some sign of altering its tight fiscal stance -- but whether that willingness exists remains to be seen.
The government plans to raise Japan's three-percent consumption tax to five percent from April 1 and has decided to end special income tax cuts aimed at boosted the economy.
Many market participants would like the consumption tax rise, which officials say is needed to help trim Japan's big budget deficit, to be delayed and the income tax cuts kept.

Critics also say the government erred in drafting its tight budget for the year from April by failing to cut spending on pet projects that benefit special interests but forging ahead with the higher tax burden plans.

"I have a personal suspicion that the Japanese government may be forced at the end of the day to modify its fiscal policy...enough to change the perception of the market," Kiuchi said. "I think the LDP cannot afford to ignore the market's demands."
